1030.title: Pakistan's Sikhs
1030.hook: Sikhs still live in Nankana Sahib, Peshawar and other towns
1030.howItsDone: Sikhs in Pakistan keep gurdwaras in Nankana Sahib, Peshawar and other towns, and on gurpurabs they host pilgrims from India and other countries; when it is open, the Kartarpur corridor lets pilgrims from India visit Kartarpur Sahib for the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Afghanistan's Sikhs, and your line was a small community. Today, Sikhs who live on the far side of a line on the map.

On the Indian side of the border, near the town of Dera Baba Nanak, there's a raised platform where pilgrims have stood with binoculars, looking across fields at a white gurdwara on the other side: Kartarpur Sahib, where tradition says Guru Nanak spent his last years farming and singing. For a long time, that look through glass was as close as many could get. Then a corridor opened that let pilgrims from India cross for the day, though it has been shut again in tense times. When they do cross, they find something the binoculars never showed: Sikhs who live there, and never left.
screen: `BINOCULARS AT THE BORDER.` → `KARTARPUR SAHIB ACROSS THE FIELDS.` → `SIKHS WHO NEVER LEFT.`

segments.voice: First, the line. When Partition divided Punjab, a border ran through the Sikh homeland, and families on both sides were uprooted in great suffering. Sikh families from the western side moved east. But the places didn't move. Second, the places. Tradition says Guru Nanak was born at Talwandi, now called Nankana Sahib. Kartarpur Sahib is where he settled. Panja Sahib holds the story of the hand on the rock. In Lahore, Gurdwara Dera Sahib marks where tradition says Guru Arjan was martyred. Much of the Sikh story's early map now lies across the border. Third, the people who stayed. Sikh families still live in Nankana Sahib, in Peshawar, and in other towns. They run shops, go to school, sit in the gurdwara, and on the great days they host pilgrims who cross from India and arrive from everywhere else. For a few days the sangat is enormous; then it's small again, and the local families keep the lamps lit. Fourth, the old song. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, at Ang 611 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru says there is one father, and we are all the children of the one. A border can decide which passport you carry. It can't decide whose child you are.
screen: `PARTITION DREW A LINE.` · `NANKANA, KARTARPUR, PANJA, DERA SAHIB.` · `FAMILIES WHO STAYED.` · `ANG 611: ONE FATHER, ONE FAMILY.` · then, large: `ACROSS THE BORDER.`

segments.voice: Picture a line on a map, any line you know, between countries, cities, or two sides of a family, and then the people on the far side of it going about an ordinary morning: opening a shop, walking a child to school, sitting in a gurdwara before work. With each breath out, let the line fade a little; if you pray, you can say Waheguru for those on both sides.
Pakistan's Sikhs. Families who still live in Nankana Sahib, Peshawar and other towns, keeping the Guru's places alive and welcoming pilgrims. Today's word.
Your line: across the border. One family of the Guru, on two sides of a line. Day one thousand thirty, and counting.

1031.title: Malaysia and Singapore
1031.hook: long-settled Sikh communities with old gurdwaras
1031.howItsDone: Sikhs in Malaysia and Singapore keep long-established gurdwaras with daily kirtan, langar and Punjabi classes, and families mark gurpurabs and Vaisakhi there as Sikhs do elsewhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pakistan's Sikhs, and your line was across the border. Today, roots that went down in warm, wet ground far from Punjab.

Afternoon rain hammers a tin roof. Ceiling fans turn slowly over a hall of people sitting cross-legged on white sheets. A harmonium and a tabla carry a hymn over the noise of the storm. Outside, frangipani trees drip, and a scooter splashes past. In the kitchen, rotis sit beside rice, because the cooks long ago learned what grows well here. This is a gurdwara in Penang, or Kuala Lumpur, or Singapore, and the families in the hall don't think of it as a new arrival. Their grandparents prayed here.
screen: `RAIN ON A TIN ROOF.` → `A HYMN OVER THE STORM.` → `THEIR GRANDPARENTS PRAYED HERE.`

segments.voice: First, the arrival. Community histories tell of Sikh men who came to Malaya and Singapore in the days of British rule, to serve in the police and as guards and watchmen, and of others who came to trade or to farm cattle. In time, wives and children followed, and a scattering of workers became a sangat. Second, the gurdwara. Community histories tell how, once a few families had settled, a place for the Guru soon followed. Some of those gurdwaras still stand, rebuilt and enlarged, with old photographs on the walls of men in turbans and uniforms. The gurdwara became the place for langar, Punjabi classes, weddings and help finding work. Third, the roots. Families here now count generations born in the tropics. Children grow up speaking English and the languages around them, and learn Punjabi in the gurdwara so they can read the Guru's words. The weather changed, the food changed a little, the language around them changed. The hymns didn't. Fourth, the line underneath. In a hymn by Guru Ram Das, at Ang 450 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru says that wherever the True Guru goes and sits, that place becomes beautiful. Some Sikhs hear in that a reason why no land is too far: where the Guru is seated and the sangat gathers, the place is made right.
screen: `POLICE, GUARDS, TRADERS, FAMILIES.` · `FIRST, A PLACE FOR THE GURU.` · `GENERATIONS BORN IN THE TROPICS.` · `ANG 450: WHERE THE GURU SITS.` · then, large: `OLD ROOTS ABROAD.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself in that hall: rain on the tin roof, fans moving warm air, white sheets, the canopy, families in rows, old photographs on the wall. Breathe in the smell of the kitchen, and on each breath out let the hymn carry over the storm. If you pray, you can say Waheguru the way the people in that hall might; if you don't, simply sit in the picture.
Gurdwara. The door of the Guru, whose old buildings in Malaysia and Singapore have held generations of Sikh families far from Punjab. Today's word.
Your line: old roots abroad. A tree that grew where it was planted. See you tomorrow.

1032.title: East Africa and Britain
1032.hook: many Sikh families moved from Kenya and Uganda to Britain
1032.howItsDone: Sikh families of East African background are part of the sangat in British gurdwaras, and some congregations were founded or grown by them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurdwara, and your line was old roots abroad. Today, families whose roots had to be pulled up and planted again.

Two journeys, one suitcase. It sits battered in a loft in an English town, with two faded labels on its side: one from Nairobi or Kampala, one from London. Inside, wrapped in cloth, are a few photographs of a house with a tin roof and a garden of mango trees, and a gutka, a small book of daily prayers, its corners soft from use. A grandmother keeps it there. Her own parents had left Punjab for East Africa. Then she left East Africa for Britain. Today is about families who moved twice.
screen: `A SUITCASE WITH TWO LABELS.` → `PUNJAB, THEN EAST AFRICA.` → `THEN BRITAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the first move. In British times, community histories say, Sikhs from Punjab went to Kenya and Uganda as craftsmen, builders and railway workers, and then as shopkeepers, teachers and civil servants. They built gurdwaras there, and children grew up who had never seen Punjab. Second, the second move. In the years after Kenya and Uganda became independent, life grew uncertain for Asian families, and in Uganda they were ordered to leave. Many Sikh families came to Britain with what they could carry. Some arrived with skills, savings or English; some arrived with very little. Third, the arrival. In towns across Britain, these families helped found and grow gurdwaras, often in old buildings bought together and made over by hand. They had done this once already, in Africa, so they knew how. Fourth, the old story. In the janamsakhis, the traditional tales of Guru Nanak, the Guru visits two villages. One treats him rudely, and he blesses it to stay where it is. The other welcomes him warmly, and he blesses it to be scattered. His companion is puzzled, and the Guru explains: let the good people scatter, so that goodness spreads wherever they go. Families who moved twice sometimes tell that story with a smile. Being scattered was hard. It was also, in that old tale, a kind of blessing.

segments.voice: Think of someone you know who has had to start again more than once, a grandparent, a neighbor, a friend from school, maybe you, and picture the boxes, the new street, the first winter. Breathe in and honor what it cost; breathe out and honor what they built anyway. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for those still unpacking; if you don't, just hold them in mind.

1033.title: North America today
1033.hook: Sikhs farm, drive, teach, heal and lead across Canada and the US
1033.howItsDone: Sikhs in Canada and the US practice kirat karni, honest work, alongside vand chakna, sharing, and gurdwaras serve langar to anyone who comes in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pardes, and your line was moved twice. Today, the people on your street, or the next one over.

Five in the morning on an interstate. A long-haul truck pulls into a rest stop, and the driver, in a neat turban, stretches and heads for coffee. A few hours later, in a valley full of orchards, a farmer checks the peach trees. In a classroom, a teacher writes the day's date on the board. In a hospital, a nurse takes a pulse. In a city council chamber, a member stands to speak. Each of them is a Sikh, and the people they pass may not think about that at all. They just think: that's my driver, my farmer, my kid's teacher, my nurse.
screen: `A TRUCK AT A REST STOP.` → `ORCHARDS, CLASSROOMS, WARDS.` → `MY DRIVER, MY TEACHER, MY NURSE.`

segments.voice: First, the work. Across Canada and the United States, Sikhs farm, drive trucks and taxis, run shops, teach, heal and serve in public office. Some families have been here for generations; some arrived last year. Second, the teaching under the work. The Sikh way calls this kirat karni, earning by honest work. Among the saloks at Ang 1376 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Namdev, a calico printer by trade, tells his friend Trilochan: with your hands and feet, do all your work, and keep your mind with the Pure One. A paycheck isn't separate from the spiritual life; it's one of its places. Third, the open door. Beside honest work, the Sikh way asks for vand chakna, sharing what you earn. Gurdwaras across the continent serve langar to anyone who walks in. Sikh volunteers have cooked for neighbors after storms and fires, and handed out meals in parking lots and stadiums. Nobody is asked what they believe before they eat. Fourth, the word. Nobody is handed the title neighbor. It grows slowly, from showing up: the driver who waves at the same diner every week, the farmer who lends a ladder over the fence, the nurse who remembers your mother's name. Sikhs in North America live it in ordinary ways, at the next desk, the next farm, the next house.
screen: `FARM, DRIVE, TEACH, HEAL, LEAD.` · `ANG 1376: HANDS AT WORK, MIND WITH GOD.` · `LANGAR FOR WHOEVER WALKS IN.` · `NEIGHBORS, MADE BY SHOWING UP.` · then, large: `NEIGHBORS.`

segments.voice: Picture the people around where you live or work: the one next door, the one across the hall, the driver, the cashier, the person who fixes things. Choose one, by name or just by face, and on each breath out thank them silently for one thing that makes your days easier. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you do.

1034.title: Standing up for rights
1034.hook: Sikh groups defend the right to wear articles of faith at work, school and in the forces
1034.howItsDone: Sikh advocacy groups help Sikhs who are told to remove a turban or kirpan at work, school or in the military, and often work alongside other faith groups on religious freedom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirat, and your line was neighbors. Today, what happens when a neighbor is told they can't come in as they are.

A schoolboy in England is offered a place at a private school, on one condition: take off the turban and cut the hair, to match the uniform. His father refuses. The family takes the school to court, loses, appeals, and the case climbs all the way to the House of Lords, then the country's highest court. There the judges decide that Sikhs are protected under Britain's race relations law, and that the school's rule was unlawful discrimination. One boy, one turban, and a ruling that reached far beyond one school gate.
screen: `TAKE OFF THE TURBAN, OR NO PLACE.` → `THE FATHER REFUSES.` → `ALL THE WAY TO THE LORDS.`

segments.voice: First, what's at stake. The Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, asks initiated Sikhs to keep the five articles of faith, among them uncut hair and the kirpan, a small sword. For a Sikh who keeps them, they're not accessories to take off for work. So when a job, a school or an army says no, it becomes a question of rights. Second, the cases. The English case was Mandla against Dowell Lee. In Canada, a student named Gurbaj Singh Multani took his school board to the Supreme Court of Canada over wearing his kirpan, and the court ruled that a total ban was not justified. In the United States, Sikh soldiers and advocacy groups such as the Sikh Coalition pressed the army to let observant Sikhs serve with turbans and beards. Third, the wider reason. Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur gave his life defending the freedom of Kashmiri Hindus to practice their own faith, not his. Sikhs remember him as standing up for someone else's right. Fourth, the line underneath. At Ang 141 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that taking what rightfully belongs to another is as forbidden as pork to a Muslim or beef to a Hindu. The word there is hakk, what rightly belongs to someone, and some Sikhs read the line widely: a right isn't a favor, and taking it away is taking something that isn't yours. Some Sikh groups argue that a ruling won for a turban protects a headscarf, a kippah and a cross as well.
screen: `ARTICLES OF FAITH, NOT ACCESSORIES.` · `ENGLAND, CANADA, THE US ARMY.` · `GURU TEGH BAHADUR, FOR OTHERS.` · `ANG 141: ANOTHER'S RIGHT.` · then, large: `RIGHTS FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose right is being quietly squeezed: someone talked over at work, someone told their name is too hard to say, someone asked to hide who they are to fit in. 1035.title: Women's voices today
1035.hook: women serve as granthis and ragis, and Sikhs discuss where women may do kirtan
1035.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, Sikh women read from the Guru Granth Sahib, sing kirtan, serve langar and sit on committees; the question of women's kirtan groups in the inner sanctum of Harmandir Sahib is still discussed within the Panth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hakk, and your line was rights for all. Today, a question Sikhs are still talking through among themselves.

Why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? That question is Guru Nanak's, in the Guru Granth Sahib. Hold it in mind. An ordinary evening in a gurdwara. A woman sits behind the Guru Granth Sahib, reading aloud, waving the chaur over the open pages. Later, a group of women sit at the harmonium and sing the evening hymns. In this hall, it's ordinary. And yet, in some places, Sikhs are still discussing where women's kirtan groups may sing. Today: a teaching that is clear, and a conversation that isn't finished.
screen: `WHY CALL HER LESSER?` → `A WOMAN AT THE GURU'S SIDE.` → `A CONVERSATION NOT FINISHED.`

segments.voice: First, the line. At Ang 473 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in a hymn of Guru Nanak, the Guru says that we are born of woman, we marry woman, through woman friendships and families are made, and then he asks: why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? The question is the teaching. Second, the practice today. Sikh women serve as granthis, reading from and caring for the Guru Granth Sahib, and as ragis, singing kirtan. Women serve on gurdwara committees, cook and serve langar, and take part in the Panj Pyare in some congregations, while others keep that role for men. The Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, opens the main parts of gurdwara life to Sikh men and women alike. Third, the open question. At Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the kirtan in the inner sanctum has traditionally been sung by men's groups, and some Sikhs have asked that women's groups sing there too. Some point to Ang 473 and say the Gurus' teaching on equality already settles it. Others say a change at that place should come through the Panth's own institutions, in their own time. The question has been raised more than once, and it is still being discussed. Fourth, the shape of it. The teaching is clear, and the practice is wide; one place, and some roles, are still under discussion. It's honest to say it's open, and honest to say whose words both sides are reaching for.

1036.title: Caste, honestly
1036.hook: the Gurus rejected caste, yet caste divisions still show in some Sikh places
1036.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, all eat together in langar sitting in one row, and the Rehat Maryada rejects caste distinctions; in some places caste still shapes marriages and gurdwara membership, and Sikh reformers work against it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan, and your line was a conversation open. Today, a harder conversation, told honestly.

In the langar hall, everyone sits on the floor in the same row: the farmer next to the doctor, the cleaner next to the landlord. That row is a sermon without words. In some villages in Punjab, you may find two gurdwaras within walking distance of each other. Same Guru, same hymns. Different families, divided by caste. A row on the floor says one thing; two buildings say another. Today is about the gap between them.
screen: `ONE ROW ON THE FLOOR.` → `TWO GURDWARAS, ONE VILLAGE.` → `THE GAP BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: First, what the Gurus said. At Ang 349 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says to recognize the divine light in everyone and not to ask about caste, because in the world beyond there is no caste. At Ang 15 he says he stands with the lowest of the low, and has nothing to do with the great. Guru Amar Das, at Ang 1127, warns: let no one be proud of caste. The Guru Granth Sahib itself holds hymns by bhagats from castes others looked down on, set beside the Gurus' own words. Second, what the Gurus did: langar and sangat, everyone in one row on one floor, and the Khalsa, where, tradition says, those who first came forward were from different castes and drank amrit from one bowl. Third, the honest part. Caste did not disappear. In some places it still shows: in separate gurdwaras, in marriages arranged within a caste, in surnames that carry old ranks, and in Sikhs from castes once called low who say they are still made to feel it. Sikh writers, reformers and Dalit Sikhs have called this out, using the Gurus' own words. And not only in villages: some diaspora towns have gurdwaras founded along caste lines too. When violence over a marriage across caste makes the news, Sikhs answer in two ways. Some say it's Punjabi culture, not Sikhi. Others say that it's a Sikh problem, whether anyone likes it or not. Both point to the same Gurus. And if anyone is in danger over a marriage, local emergency help comes first. Fourth, the line. A path isn't judged only by how well its followers keep it; it also gives them a standard. On caste, that standard is not in doubt.
screen: `ANG 349: DON'T ASK ABOUT CASTE.` · `ONE ROW, ONE FLOOR, ONE BOWL.` · `CASTE STILL SHOWS IN SOME PLACES.` · `THE STANDARD IS NOT IN DOUBT.` · then, large: `THE GURUS REJECTED IT.`

segments.voice: People get sorted by accent, job, family name; gently ask whether you sort anyone without meaning to, and look at it plainly, without punishing yourself. Then picture yourself in the langar row beside the very person that bias would put elsewhere, and stay a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Caste. A ranking of people by birth, rejected by the Gurus in word and practice, and still showing in some Sikh places. Today's word.
Your line: the gurus rejected it. The work is in the gap between the hymn and the village. Day one thousand thirty-six.
